content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has updated its 2010 guidelines on improving access to health workers in rural and remote areas through enhanced retention strategies. These guidelines focus on health workforce development, recruitment, and retention in underserved areas. The updated recommendations are evidence-based and aim to address the challenges of health worker distribution within countries, emphasizing strategies to attract, recruit, and retain health professionals in rural and remote regions. The guidelines are publicly available under a Creative Commons license, allowing non-commercial use, adaptation, and redistribution, provided proper citation is given. However, the use of the WHO logo is prohibited, and any adaptations must be licensed under similar terms. Translations of the guidelines must include a disclaimer stating that WHO is not responsible for the accuracy or content of the translation, with the original English version being the authoritative edition. The guidelines are part of WHO’s broader efforts to support health workforce optimization and universal health coverage. They align with other WHO initiatives, such as the 2013 guidelines on transforming and scaling up health professionals’ education and training, which emphasize producing graduates responsive to population health needs. These educational reforms are closely tied to rural retention strategies. The WHO Global Code of Practice on the International Recruitment of Health Personnel, adopted in 2010, complements these guidelines by addressing international health worker mobility and promoting equitable health workforce distribution. The guidelines also reference the importance of addressing workplace violence in the health sector, as outlined in the 2002 framework developed by WHO, the International Labour Organization (ILO), and other partners. This framework provides general guidance for developing culturally and contextually appropriate tools to address workplace violence. A forthcoming WHO guidebook on health labor market analysis will further support countries in identifying gaps in health worker distribution and implementing policy actions to address these disparities. This analysis can also monitor progress in improving the geographic distribution of health workers. The guidelines include specific recommendations based on the PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome) framework. These recommendations address various strategies, such as: 1. Locating health professional schools and training programs in rural areas to increase the likelihood of graduates working in these regions. 2. Exposing undergraduate health students to rural community experiences and clinical rotations to encourage rural practice. 3. Including rural health topics in curricula to enhance competencies and retention of health professionals in rural areas. 4. Providing accessible continuing education and professional development programs tailored to rural health workers. 5. Expanding the scope of practice for rural health workers to improve retention. 6. Introducing new types of health workers with appropriate training and regulation for rural practice. 7. Ensuring compulsory rural service is accompanied by adequate support and incentives. 8. Offering scholarships, bursaries, or subsidies with enforceable return-of-service agreements to increase rural recruitment and retention. 9. Improving living conditions, infrastructure, and services for health workers and their families in rural areas. 10. Providing a safe and secure working environment to enhance retention. 11. Offering sustainable financial incentives, such as hardship allowances, housing grants, and paid vacations. 12. Establishing professional networks, rural health associations, and journals to support rural health workers. 13. Recognizing rural health workers through public awards and titles to improve motivation and retention. The guidelines were developed with input from a diverse group of experts, including academics, policymakers, and representatives from civil society and international organizations. The recommendations are categorized by their strength and the quality of evidence supporting them. For example, targeting rural background students and implementing rural-based curricula are strongly recommended based on moderate to low-quality evidence. Other strategies, such as compulsory service and return-of-service agreements, are conditionally recommended due to low-quality evidence. Overall, the updated WHO guidelines provide a comprehensive framework for addressing the challenges of health workforce distribution and retention in rural and remote areas, contributing to the progressive realization of universal health coverage.
